profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review between a faculty lead and a research engineer for an internal proposal that extends a recent benchmark on neural-network quantum states for global quench dynamics in a non-integrable quantum Ising chain. The team wants to decide whether the proposed benchmark design is solid enough to justify a new GPU allocation request and to support a workshop paper comparing RBM and neural autoregressive ansatz families on how representation size scales with evolution time. The agenda is to review the proposed benchmark framing, the definition of the scaling curve, the reference trajectory to compare against, and whether the comparison protocol is sufficiently architecture-agnostic. The expected outcome is a light approval of the design with implementation responsibilities assigned, without reopening the headline choices of quench setting, model families, or primary metric.

members.name: Dr. Lena Hoffmann
members.role: Principal Investigator, Quantum Machine Learning Group
members.expertise: Variational quantum dynamics, neural-network quantum states, benchmark methodology
members.background: A theoretical physicist who led the group's earlier paper on neural-network quantum states for quench dynamics and now oversees follow-up studies intended for publication.
members.private_state: She wants the benchmark extension to look methodologically conservative and comparable to the group's prior paper so that any new result is interpretable and easy to defend in review; she is also wary of hidden degrees of freedom in the evaluation protocol that could make architecture comparisons look inflated.
hidden_assumptions: When people say "parameter count," they mean the number of unique trainable weights in the ansatz, not auxiliary stored tensors or replicated position-specific parameters introduced by implementation details.

The phrase "given accuracy at time t" means the model family has stayed under the stated error threshold throughout the trajectory up to t, because the scientific claim is about how long the dynamics remain representable.

The "reference trajectory" for this benchmark is the exact-diagonalization trajectory on the small-chain Ising setup used in the earlier paper, even if larger-system approximate trajectories exist internally.

A "fair comparison" across architectures means using essentially the same optimizer schedule and training recipe, with only minimal scaling changes, so representation differences are not confounded with tuning effort.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: Large-scale model training, autoregressive architectures, experiment infrastructure for physics ML
members.background: He builds and runs the group's training pipelines, recently migrated their benchmark code to support larger-system TEBD references and more architecture-specific training configurations.
members.private_state: He wants approval for a design that makes practical use of the newer infrastructure and larger-system runs already on disk, and he prefers reporting conventions that match how experiments are actually selected and stored in the pipeline.
hidden_assumptions: When people ask for "parameter count," they usually want the effective stored model size per run as instantiated in code, including embeddings, output heads, and other learned tensors that occupy memory and affect training footprint.

The phrase "given accuracy at time t" refers to whether there exists a trained checkpoint for that time whose selected evaluation score meets the threshold, not necessarily whether every earlier point on the trajectory also met it.

The "reference trajectory" for the current benchmark naturally means the newer 80-site TEBD trajectory used in the updated pipeline, with exact diagonalization serving only as a sanity check where possible.
A "fair comparison" means each architecture is allowed its own tuned learning-rate schedule and training settings as long as the overall compute budget is comparable.
Implementation-facing quantities reported to the cluster request should align with what the training system logs automatically, even if that differs from older paper conventions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to plot "parameter count versus time" for each ansatz family.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the number of unique trainable weights that define the ansatz class, excluding implementation-specific replicated tensors, optimizer state, and bookkeeping components.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the total learned model footprint logged by the code for each run, including site embeddings, separate output blocks, and other stored trainable tensors that are part of the instantiated model.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations sound standard in ML practice, and because neither person is debating the plot itself, the counting convention feels too obvious to restate during a design review.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to achieve a given accuracy at time t
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss how many parameters are required "at a given accuracy" as time increases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 interprets this as the smallest model size for which the trajectory remains below the error threshold continuously up to time t, since the scientific claim concerns the time horizon of faithful simulation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 interprets this as the smallest model size for which the selected checkpoint for that specific probed time t meets the threshold, even if earlier or neighboring times would fail under the same setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase comes directly from the paper-style framing and sounds precise enough on the surface, so neither expects a hidden difference in whether the threshold is pointwise-at-t or cumulative-through-t.

misalignment_points.topic: Which reference trajectory they are benchmarking against
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to using "the reference trajectory from the Ising quench" for the comparison.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the exact-diagonalization trajectory on the small system from the earlier published setup, which she treats as the canonical benchmark reference.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the newer 80-site TEBD trajectory generated in the updated pipeline, which he considers the default reference for current experiments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both trajectories come from the same nominal quench setup and are familiar inside the group, so the phrase "the reference trajectory" creates a strong false sense that there is only one obvious object being discussed.

misalignment_points.topic: What a fair comparison protocol entails
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the architectures should be compared using "the same recipe" or a "fair comparison."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a shared optimizer family and nearly identical schedule across model classes, so the benchmark isolates representation scaling rather than optimization craftsmanship.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means equalized compute budgets while allowing architecture-specific hyperparameter schedules and training tricks, because that is the practical way to make different models competitive.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are common senses of fairness in ML benchmarking, and the review is focused on whether the design is generally acceptable, not on enumerating every low-level training setting.
